column2: Then the Gautami, the refuge, pleased, joyfully spoke to Gautama, who was with the old woman, humble and distressed and seeking refuge:

Sprinkle your wife with my waters joined with mantras, with pitchers and offerings; then your beloved wife
brahmapuran:107:60	will obtain a lovely form — beautiful, graceful in every limb, fortunate, with lovely eyes, endowed with every good mark.
brahmapuran:107:61	And you, sprinkled in turn by your beautiful wife, will obtain a lovely form endowed with every good mark.
Saying "So be it" at the Ganga's words, the two did as instructed, and both obtained beauty by the grace of the Gautami.
The water of that sprinkling became a river, famed by the name of the old woman, O best of sages.
It is famed as the river Vriddha, and Gautama too was called Vriddha Gautama by the sages who dwelt with him. The old woman said to the Gautami Ganga, present in visible form:

O goddess, let this river be called by my name, Vriddha; its confluence with you will be an unsurpassed holy place,
brahmapuran:107:66	increasing beauty, good fortune, wealth, sons and grandsons, long life, health and well-being, victory and affection, and by bathing, giving and fire offerings supremely purifying the ancestors.
So be it, said the Ganga to that old woman, beloved of Gautama. The linga installed by Gautama is praised by the name Vriddha.
There the best of sages found joy with the old woman; bathing and giving there grant every wish.
From then on that holy place is called the confluence of Vriddha.
If you do not fall from battle, where will you go if you flee? At the Yaksha's words the king of kings fought in anger.
Having conquered Yakshas of many kinds, he stayed ten nights; the lord of the Yakshas, becoming a deer, lived in the forest with his wife.
His house taken, his servants taken, he had gone to the forest; anxious, he said to his beloved Yaksha wife, who had taken the form of a doe:

This king is ill-intentioned, beloved, his mind given to vice; how may he come to misfortune? Think of a means for that.
brahmapuran:108:23	The kingdoms of all rulers end in sinful pursuits and vices. Lure him to Uma's forest, fair-browed one, becoming a charming doe.
brahmapuran:108:24	If this king enters there, he will become a woman without doubt. You must do it, dear one; it is not fitting for me, for I am a man, while you are a woman and a Yakshi.
Why should you not go to the unsurpassed forest of Uma? What fault would there be if you went? Tell me truly.

On the Himalaya, best of mountains, Shiva with Uma, surrounded by gods and hosts, roamed at pleasure. Once Parvati said to Shankara when he was alone:
brahmapuran:108:27	'It is the nature of women that love-play should be kept hidden; therefore give me a secure place protected by your command.
brahmapuran:108:28	Give me, lord of the gods, the place known as Uma's forest. Except for you, Ganesha, Karttikeya and Nandin,
brahmapuran:108:29	whoever enters here, Lord, let him become a woman.'
brahmapuran:108:30	Thus was the command given concerning Uma's forest by the pleased moon-crested god. What can I do, being a man, beloved, pressed by your love? Therefore I must not go to Uma's excellent forest.
Hearing her husband's words, the Yakshi, able to take any form, became a wide-eyed doe and appeared before Ila.
The Yaksha stayed there; Ila then saw the doe, and his mind, attached to hunting, was especially drawn by the doe.
Alone, mounted on his horse, he went out after that doe; slowly she drew on the king, eager for the hunt.
Slowly she went to the place called Uma's forest, the doe showing herself to him here and there, then unseen,
stopping, going, running as if afraid; that doe with restless eyes drew him to Uma's forest.
Following on horseback, he reached Uma's forest. Knowing that he had entered Uma's forest, the Yakshi then
abandoned the doe's form and, able to take any form, assumed a divine form near an ashoka tree,
her hand resting on its branch, anointed with divine perfume, bearing a divine form, slender, her task accomplished.
Laughing, she looked at the king, weary on his horse, and at Ila, his eyes restless, looking for the doe;
remembering all her husband's words, she said to the king:
Slender woman on horseback, where are you going alone? In the dress of a man, Ila, whom will you follow?
Hearing the word "Ila," the king swooned with anger; reproaching the Yakshi, he asked her again about the doe.
Still the Yakshi said, "Ila, what are you looking for?" Hearing "Ila," the one on horseback, holding his bow,
angrily showed his bow, conqueror of the three worlds. Again she said to the great-souled king, "Ila, look at yourself,
then tell me whether I, truthful, am false." Then the king saw two high breasts on his chest,
and was astonished: "What is this that has happened to me?"
What is this that has happened to me? You know it clearly; tell me everything as it is, and who you are, O woman of good vows.

In the best of Himalayan caves dwells my husband, angry, the glorious lord of the Yakshas; I am his wife, a Yakshi.
brahmapuran:108:49	You, the king, sat in his very cool cave, whose Yakshas you slew in delusion without a proper battle.
brahmapuran:108:50	Then, to get you out, I became a doe and entered Uma's forest, and you have entered. Long ago Maheshvara said,
brahmapuran:108:51	'Whatever foolish man enters here will become a woman'; therefore you have become a woman. You should not grieve; even the wise — who here knows the strangeness of destiny?
Hearing the Yakshi's words, the rider fell from the horse; comforting him, the same Yakshi spoke again:
Womanhood has come and is here; you cannot make it manhood. Take the knowledge fit for a woman — dance, song, adornment, feminine grace, feminine charm and all a woman's ways.
Ila, having obtained all of it, said to the Yakshi:
Who will be my husband, what must I do, and how may manhood come again? Tell me this, auspicious one, for I am especially distressed; nothing is better than relieving the distress of the distressed.

Budha, son of Soma, has his hermitage east of this forest, fair one; he goes daily to his father.
brahmapuran:108:57	By this very path the planet Budha goes daily to see and to bow to his father Soma.
brahmapuran:108:58	When the tranquil Budha comes, show yourself; seeing him, fair one, you will obtain all desires.
Having comforted her, the fair-browed Yakshi vanished; the Yakshi told her husband, and the Yaksha too was happy.
Ila's army that was there went away as it pleased. Staying in Uma's forest, Ila sang and danced again and again,
acting in a woman's ways, remembering the course of karma. Once, while Ila was dancing,
the wise Budha, setting out to go to his father, saw her. Seeing Ila, abandoning his journey, Budha came to her and said:
Be my wife, at ease; be dearest to me of all.
Ila devotedly welcomed Budha's words and did so; remembering the Yakshi's words, she was then pleased, O sage.
Budha delighted in her lovingly, taking her to his excellent abode; and she pleased her husband with all her heart. Then, after many days, Budha, pleased, said to his beloved:
What shall I give you, dear one, that is dear and in your mind?
At the very moment of his words, Ila said to Budha, son of Soma, loving and dear, "Give me a son."

This seed of mine is unfailing and born of love; therefore you will have a son, a kshatriya famed in the world,
brahmapuran:108:69	founder of the lunar line, glorious, like the sun in splendour, equal to Brihaspati in intellect and to the earth in forbearance,
brahmapuran:108:70	like Hari in valour in battle and like fire in anger.
When that great-souled son of Budha was being born, cries of victory arose everywhere, even in the abode of the gods.
When Budha's son was born, the lords of the gods came there; I too came there joyfully, O wise one.
As soon as he was born the son made a loud cry; at that all the assembled sages and gods said:
Since his cry (rava) is loud (puru), let him be Pururavas — so all, content in mind, gave him the name.
Budha taught his son the auspicious science of the kshatriya; Budha gave his son the science of archery with its practice.
He grew quickly like the moon in the bright fortnight. Seeing his mother Ila full of sorrow, the wise son of Ila bowed humbly and said to Ila:
Mother, Budha is my father and your beloved husband, and I am your capable son; why is there a fever in your mind?

True, my son, Budha is my husband and you are my son, a mine of virtue; I never have any worry on account of husband or son.
brahmapuran:108:79	Yet, remembering again and again some former sorrow, I brood, O wise one. Then he said to his mother:
Tell me that first, Mother.
And Ila said to him, "How can I tell a secret? Yet I tell you, my son, since a son is the refuge of his parents; for those sunk in the ocean of sorrow, a son is the best boat."
Hearing his mother's words, humbly, falling at her feet, he said to his mother, "Tell me as it is, Mother."
She told Pururavas of the Ikshvaku family, her birth there, her own name, gaining the kingdom, her dear sons,
the family priest Vasishtha, her beloved wife, her own position, the going out to the forest, the sending of the ministers and priest
to the city, the passion for hunting, the going to the Himalayan cave, to the house of the lord of the Yakshas,
entering Uma's forest and attaining womanhood in full, and that by Maheshvara's command no man may enter there,
the Yakshi's words and her boon, meeting Budha, their love and the birth of a son — all of it
she told him. Hearing it, Pururavas said to his mother: "What shall I do? By doing what would there be merit?
If you are satisfied with this much, enough, Mother; but if there is anything else in your mind, command me that too."

I would wish for excellent manhood, the best kingdom, and the consecration of my sons and especially of you,
brahmapuran:108:91	to give gifts, to sacrifice, to see the path of liberation — I wish to do all this by your grace, my son.
brahmapuran:108:92	I ask you the means by which I may obtain manhood, by austerity or otherwise; tell me truly.
Go and ask your father Budha, my son, truly; he knows everything and will teach you what is good.
At his mother's words the son of Ila went quickly to his father and, bowing, told of his mother's task and his own.

I know Ila, O wise one, and Ila as she was born again, the entering of Uma's forest and Shambhu's command.
brahmapuran:108:96	Therefore by the grace of Shambhu and of Uma the curse will be lifted, my son, by worshipping those two and not otherwise.
How may I see that god and the Mother Shiva? By a holy place or by austerity? Tell me that first, father.
Go to the Gautami, my son; there Shiva always dwells with Uma, glorious, remover of curses, giver of boons.
Hearing his father's words, Pururavas rejoiced; the wise one set out for austerity at the Gautami, the Ganga, purifier of the three worlds,
desiring manhood for his mother, hastening to austerity, having bowed to the Himalaya mountain, his mother, father and teacher.
As the son went, Ila and Soma's son followed; they all reached the Gautami from the Himalaya, best of mountains.
Having bathed there and performed some austerity, they offered supreme praise to Bhava, god of gods; hear this order of praise:
Budha praised first, then Ila, then the son Pururavas praised the goddess Gauri and Shankara:

Those two who with saffron from their own bodies are naturally like golden images, alike in form, worshipped by Skanda and the lord of the Ganas — may they, the refuges, be my refuge.
brahmapuran:108:105	Those two by thinking of whom embodied beings burned by the forest fire of the threefold suffering of worldly existence at once attain supreme bliss — may those auspicious ones be my refuge.
brahmapuran:108:106	I am distressed, my mind oppressed; there is no other protector from affliction; O god, your most holy feet — may they, the refuges, be my refuge.
brahmapuran:108:107	From whom all this arises and into whom at the end it dissolves — the refuges of the world whose self is the world, Gauri and Hara, may they be my refuge.
brahmapuran:108:108	Those feet of the mountain's daughter which Shiva out of love held at the great festival among the hosts of gods, saying 'Take them, O Lord' — may they, the refuges, be my refuge.
What wish shall I grant you? Tell me; you are fulfilled; blessings on you, even what is hard for the gods.
King Ila entered the forest without knowing your command, Mother; forgive that, queen of the gods; you should grant manhood.
So be it, she said to them all, abiding by Bhava's will; then the Lord, ever delighting in the Goddess's words, said:
By merely being sprinkled here, let this king obtain manhood.
When Budha's wife bathed, water flowed from her body; the dance, song and beauty that had been acquired from the Yakshi
all entered the Ganga's water in streams; these became the rivers Nritya, Gita and Saubhagya.
They too joined the Ganga — those three holy confluences; bathing and giving at them grant the fruit of kingship among the gods.
Ila, having obtained manhood by the grace of Gauri and Shambhu, then performed a horse sacrifice for the attainment of great prosperity.
Bringing the family priest Vasishtha, his wife and sons, ministers, army and treasury, that best of kings
established the fourfold army and kingdom in Dandaka; that city is famed there by the name of Ila.
Having consecrated the sons born before in the kingdom descending in the solar line, he afterwards, out of love, consecrated the son of Ila,
Let this glorious one be king, founder of the lunar line; of all those wise ones he became the eldest and best, O sage.
Where King Ila's auspicious sacrifices took place, where he obtained manhood, where the sons gathered,
where dance, song, good fortune and blessings given by the Yakshi became rivers and joined the Ganga — those, O Narada,
became sixteen thousand auspicious holy places on both banks, my child; there Shambhu is Ileshvara; bathing and giving at them grant the fruit of all sacrifices.
Then, when the gods had gone, Vishnu, eager for the discus, went to the Godavari and began to worship Shambhu.
With a thousand divine, fragrant golden lotuses Vishnu devotedly performed his daily worship of the husband of Uma.
As he worshipped thus, hear the truth of the two: when one of the thousand lotuses was missing,

the enemy of the Asuras plucked out his own eye and prepared it as the offering; taking the offering-vessel with the thousand lotuses in hand and meditating on Shambhu, Hari, having no other refuge, gave the offering:
You alone, O god, know the feeling within men; you alone are the refuge and the Lord; what deliberation can there be here?
Saying this, with tears in his eyes, he became absorbed in the Lord; then Shambhu with Bhavani appeared before him.
Embracing Hari tightly, he filled him with various boons; that very eye became the discus, and the eye too was as before.
Then all the hosts of gods praised Hari and Shankara, the Ganga, best of rivers, and the bull-bannered god.
From then on that holy place is remembered as Chakratirtha, by merely hearing of which one is freed from all sins.
Whoever bathes, gives and offers libations to the ancestors there is freed from all sins and shares heaven with the ancestors; that holy place marked with the discus is seen even today.

For those who know the scriptures, who are established in the highest truth and have lost attachment to worldly activity, what use is devotion to another's affairs, O sage, by which there is no happiness here or hereafter?
brahmapuran:110:27	The enemies of the gods will turn their hatred on the place where they are kept, O best of brahmins; listen. If the weapons are lost or stolen, O lord of sages, the gods will become angry and become your enemies.
brahmapuran:110:28	Therefore, best of Veda-knowers, it is not fitting to claim another's property as one's own; friendship lasts only as long as the property; when it is lost or stolen, they become enemies.
brahmapuran:110:29	If one has the power to give wealth, it should simply be given to the one who asks — what is there to consider? Otherwise the good should do others' tasks by words, thoughts and deeds.
brahmapuran:110:30	Holding another's property is rejected by the good; give it up at once, beloved.
Hearing his beloved's words, the brahmin said to his fair-browed wife:
Having formerly agreed with the gods, dear one, saying 'no' does not please me.
Hearing what her husband said, the beloved fell silent, thinking that nothing but fate is powerful for men; the best of gods, having deposited their exceedingly radiant weapons,

bowed to the lord of sages and went to their worlds, the enemies of the Daityas, their weapons laid down and their purpose fulfilled. When the gods had gone, the best of sages lived happily and righteously with his wife.
When a long time had passed, a thousand divine years by count, those gods, O lord of sages, gave no word or thought to the weapons.
Dadhichi said to Gabhastini: "By their might the enemies of the gods hate me here, dear one; the gods do not wish to take back what they deposited here; tell me what is fitting."
She said to her beloved humbly: "What was said has been said; you know, Lord, what is fitting here. The Daityas, greatly grown, strong in austerity and power, will steal these weapons."
To protect the weapons he did this: he washed them with mantras and holy water, and that very holy water, containing all the weapons and full of splendour, Dadhichi drank.
Those weapons, powerless in form, gradually perished through the working of time. The gods came and said to Dadhichi, "Great danger from our enemies has come.
Give us the weapons, foremost of sages, which the gods deposited with you." Dadhichi said, "Out of fear of the gods' enemies, and since you did not come for so long,
the weapons have been drunk and rest in my body; tell me what is fitting." Hearing his words, the gods, bowed with humility, said to him:

We can only say 'give us the weapons,' and nothing else in reply, O lord of sages. Without them we shall always be overcome; our enemies are strong — where shall we go, lord of sages?
brahmapuran:110:43	There will be no dwelling for the gods today in the mortal world, below, or in heaven, dear one; you are the best of brahmins and endowed with austerity; nothing else is fit for us to say before you.

Then the brahmin said, "Let them take the weapons that rest in my bones; there is no doubt of this." The gods said to him, "What use is this to us? Without weapons the lords of the gods have become like women."
Then again the foremost of sages said, "Joined in yoga, I will give up the life-breaths of my body; let them make weapons from my bones, unsurpassed and of excellent form."
Do so, they said to Dadhichi of undaunted spirit, giving this fire-like answer; at that time his beloved, Pratitheyi, was not present, O lord of sages.
Those gods, not seeing her and afraid of her, quickly said to the brahmin, "Do it." Full of love he gave up his life-breaths, so hard to give up: "Enjoy this body as you please;
may all the gods be pleased with my bones; what use is the body?"

Having said this, seated in the lotus posture, his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose, bright and serene, drawing the breath with the fire slowly by the yoga of opening the middle channel into the space of the heart,
placing his mind on that immeasurable supreme state, whose form is Brahman, which is to be worshipped, the great soul attained union with Brahman.
Seeing his body lifeless, the gods quickly said to Tvashtri, "Make many weapons at once."
He said to them, "How can this be done with a brahmin's body here, O gods? I fear to do so dreadful a thing; I cannot. Excellent weapons would have to be cut out.
I will make them at once from the bones." Then the gods hastily said to the cows:
Your mouths are being made thunderbolts for our good; O cows, in a moment for the gods' weapons, tear apart Dadhichi's body and give us the pure bones today.
At the gods' words they did so; licking the flesh away, they gave the bones to the gods; the gods of undaunted spirit went quickly to their abode, and so did the cows.
Having made the weapons for the gods, Tvashtri went away at the gods' command. Then, after a long time, the virtuous and gentle Subhadra, the husband's beloved, pregnant with a child, hastening,
with a pitcher full of water in her hand, having bowed to Uma and come with fruits and flowers, wishing to see the fire, her husband and the hermitage, came back quickly.
As Pratitheyi was coming, a falling meteor warned her; she came in agitation to her own hermitage and did not see her husband before her.
Where has he gone? In astonishment Pratitheyi asked the fire; then the fire told her in detail of the gods' coming and their request for his body,
the taking of the bones and his departure; hearing all, she was grief-stricken, and from the shock of sorrow she fell to the ground, and was slowly comforted by the fire.
I am not able to curse the immortals; I will enter the fire; what else is there for me to do?
Restraining her anger and grief, the virtuous woman then spoke the righteous words of her husband:

Whatever is born is perishable; in the human world there is nothing to grieve over. Meritorious people give up their dear lives here for the sake of cows, brahmins and gods.
brahmapuran:110:64	As the wheel of worldly existence turns, having obtained a capable, righteous body, blessed are those living beings who give up their dear lives for the sake of gods and brahmins.
brahmapuran:110:65	All the life-breaths of anyone who has a body will depart; there is not the slightest doubt. Knowing this, the lordly ones give them up for the sake of brahmins, cows, gods, the poor and others.
brahmapuran:110:66	Though I, devoted to him, would have prevented him, he accepted the gods' weapons. Who knows the mind of the Creator, or of one whose deeds surpass the mortal world?
Having said this and duly worshipped the fires, she entered them with her husband's skin and hair; Pratitheyi, cutting open her womb and taking the child in her hand,
having bowed to the Ganga, the earth, the hermitage, and the trees and plants of the hermitage, said:

This child is bereft of father, of kinsmen of his lineage, and of mother; let all the hosts of beings, the plants and the guardians of the worlds protect this child.
brahmapuran:110:70	Those who look upon and protect a child bereft of mother and father as no different from one grown from their own body are surely to be revered even by Brahma and the others.
Having said this, devoted to her husband's mind, she left the child; placing the child near the pippala trees and bowing,
circumambulating the fire, with the sacrificial vessels, Pratitheyi entered the fire and went to heaven with her husband.
Those dwelling in the hermitage and the forest trees wept — those who had been nourished like sons by the sage Dadhichi:
Without him we will not live, nor without that mother. The deer, all the birds and the trees said to one another:

Those who show unfailing, genuine love to the children of parents who have gone to heaven are indeed the accomplished ones.
brahmapuran:110:76	As Dadhichi and Pratitheyi looked after us before, so neither father nor mother does now; shame on us, we are sinners.
brahmapuran:110:77	From now on this is settled for all of us: the child is Dadhichi, the child is Pratitheyi, the child is eternal dharma.
Having said this, the plants together with the trees went to King Soma and asked for the excellent nectar.
Soma gave them the unsurpassed nectar, and they gave the child the nectar dear to the gods.
Satisfied by it, he grew like the moon in the bright fortnight; since he was protected by the pippalas, the child was Pippalada. Grown up, he said to the pippalas, greatly astonished:
Humans are born from humans, birds from birds, plants from seeds; no irregularity is seen in the world. How was I born of a tree, alive with hands, feet and so on?
The trees, hearing his words, told him everything in order: Dadhichi's death, the virtuous wife's entering the fire,
the gods' taking of the bones — all this in detail. Hearing it, overcome with grief, he fell to the ground.
Comforted again by the trees with words full of dharma and meaning, recovered, he spoke again to the plants and trees:

I will kill my father's killers; I cannot live otherwise. A son follows his father's friends and enemies alike.
brahmapuran:110:86	He alone is a son; another is remembered as an enemy in a son's form. Friends of one's father, they say, save even the hostile.
The trees took the child and went to Soma; the trees told Soma the child's words; hearing them, Soma spoke to the child Pippalada:
Take all knowledge duly, the wealth of austerity and auspicious speech; you will obtain valour, beauty, strength and intellect, my son, by my command.
Pippalada humbly said to the lord of plants:

I consider all this vain until I bring retribution on my father's killers; therefore tell me that first:
brahmapuran:110:91	in what land, at what time, with what deity and mantra, at what holy place my resolve may be accomplished, O best of gods.
The Moon, after meditating long, said: "Whether enjoyment or liberation, all comes from the god Maheshvara; there is no doubt."
He said to Soma again: "How shall I see Maheshvara? I am a child with a child's mind; I have no power or austerity."

Go to the Gautami, dear one, and praise Hara, lord of the discus; the Lord will be pleased with you with little effort, my child.
brahmapuran:110:95	Mahadeva, compassionate Shiva himself, will be pleased; Shambhu stays there, seen face to face by the mighty Vishnu,
brahmapuran:110:96	and he gave Vishnu a boon and the discus worshipped by the gods. Go there, wise one, to the river Gautami in Dandaka.
brahmapuran:110:97	The plants know the holy place called Chakreshvara; go there and praise Shankara, lord of the gods, with all your heart; pleased with you, my child, he will grant all your desires.
At the king's words, O Brahman, the great sage Pippalada came to where Rudra, lord of the world, the giver of the discus, was.

The pippalas, full of compassion for the child, went to their own hermitages. Then, having bathed in the Godavari and bowed to the lord of the three worlds, the pure Pippalada praised Shiva with all his heart:

I bow to Shambhu, the primal god, to whom the steadfast, abandoning all actions and desires, having conquered the winds of the mind, go with effort for refuge to obtain liberation.
brahmapuran:110:101	May he who is witness of all, the inner self of all, lord of all, treasury of all arts, knowing all that is in my mind, the enemy of Love, show me compassion.
brahmapuran:110:102	When the ten-headed one, having conquered the lords of the quarters, shook Kailasa of the enemy of the cities worshipped by the gods, he was sent down below Rasatala merely by the pressure of his toe;
brahmapuran:110:103	hearing the words of that one whose body was crushed, you laughed with the Goddess and gave him what he wished; pleased, and even when angry, you are thus a giver even to the unworthy, O Maheshvara.
brahmapuran:110:104	He who always worshipped Hara exceedingly obtained the prosperity of the Sautramani; Bana, praiseworthy, performed a lofty, delightful and charming worship of the one crowned with the crescent moon.
brahmapuran:110:105	Having conquered his enemies and honoured the hosts of gods, Vishakha went to bow to his father; he became angry seeing the lord of the Ganas carried on his lap, and Soma, placing him on his lap, laughed.
brahmapuran:110:106	Though seated on the Lord's lap, the child by a child's nature did not leave his mother's lap; unable to pacify his angry son, Soma then took the half-woman form.
Then the Self-born, well pleased, said to Pippalada:
Choose a boon as you wish, Pippalada; blessings on you.

O Mahadeva, my illustrious father was slain by the gods — without pretence and truthful — and likewise my mother, faithful to her husband.
brahmapuran:110:110	Having heard in detail of their death at the hands of the gods, Lord, overcome with grief and anger, I cannot bear to live.
brahmapuran:110:111	Therefore give me the power to destroy the gods; you alone in the three worlds are to be served and cannot be slain, O moon-crested one.
If you are able to look at my third eye, sinless one, then you will be able to cut down the gods.
Then he set his mind to looking at the Lord's third eye; he could not, and then said to Shankara, "I am not able."
Perform some austerity, child; when you see the third eye, then you will obtain your wish without doubt.
Hearing the Lord's words and resolved on austerity, the righteous son of Dadhichi stayed there many years,
wholly absorbed in meditation on Shiva, a child yet like one strong; rising each morning, bathing and bowing to his elders in order,
seated comfortably, placing his mind in the Sushumna with single focus, placing his hands crossed at the navel, forgetting worldly existence,
he meditated on Shambhu's splendour rising from centre to centre; Pippalada saw the god's third eye and, bowing with joined palms, humbly said:

Shambhu, god of gods, formerly gave me a boon: 'The moment you see the light of my third eye,
brahmapuran:110:120	all you ask will be accomplished,' said the lord of the gods. Therefore give me what will be the cause of my enemies' destruction.
At that very moment the pippalas said, "O radiant one, your mother Pratitheyi, a mare too, has gone to heaven, they say.
Men devoted to harming others, forgetting their own good, their minds wandering here and there, fall into the pit of hell."
Hearing these words of his mothers, Pippalada became angry; when pride burns within, good counsel is useless.
Give, give! he said to him; a Kritya came forth from the eye; the brahmin remembering the mare, the Kritya too had the form of a mare,
bearing abundant fire within for the destruction of all beings — like Gabhastini, pregnant with a child, the mother of Pippalada.
Through the yoga of his meditation the Kritya was born pregnant with fire, very terrible, fearsome like the tongue of death.
She said to Pippalada, "What is my task? Tell me that." Pippalada said to her, "Devour the gods, my enemies."
Saying "So be it," she seized Pippalada who stood before her. He said, "What is this, Kritya?" and she said, "As you said:
your body was made by the gods." Then, afraid, he went to Shiva; the sage praised the god, and then Shiva spoke to the Kritya:
By my command do not seize the beings dwelling within a yojana; therefore go far from here, Kritya, and then do your task.
A yojana east of the Pippala holy place, the Kritya created by the sage stood in the form of a mare.
In her was born a great fire, able to destroy the worlds; seeing it, all the gods, terrified, went to Shambhu,
to Chakreshvara, Pippalesha, pleased by Pippalada; praising him with fearful minds, the dwellers of heaven said to Shambhu:

Protect us, Shambhu; the Kritya and her fire oppress us; be the refuge, lord of all, giver of fearlessness to the frightened.
brahmapuran:110:135	For all creatures overcome on every side, distressed and weary-minded, you alone are the refuge, Shiva.
brahmapuran:110:136	The Kritya, requested by the sage, came out of the fire of your eye; she wishes to kill the three worlds; you are our protector and no other.
The lord of the world said to them: "The Kritya does not harm those who dwell within a yojana; therefore, immortals, stay here day and night, and you will have no fear of her."
They said again to the lord of the gods: "Heaven was given by you; how can we leave it and dwell here, Lord, worshipped by the gods?"
Hearing the gods' words, Shiva then said:

That god whose eyes are everywhere, whose faces are everywhere, who blows with his rays and is ever regarded as the begetter —
brahmapuran:110:142	let that Sun alone always stay here in visible form; all of you will abide in his form.
Saying "So be it" at Shambhu's words, the gods made the Sun of the Parijata tree; Tvashtri said to the Sun:
Stay right here, lord of the world, and protect these gods yourself; we too will stay here with our portions near Shambhu.
Around Chakreshvara, for a yojana, reaching both banks of the Ganga, the best of gods stayed.
Occupying the Ganga's bank every half of a half finger-breadth, there are three crores and five hundred holy places, O best of sages; who can hear or tell their glory?
Then all the hosts of gods humbly said to Shiva:
Pacify Pippalada, lord of the gods, you who are the world.
Saying "Om," the lord of the world said to Pippalada:

Even if the gods are destroyed, your father will not come back. Your father gave his life for the accomplishment of the gods' task.
brahmapuran:110:151	Who in existence could be such a kinsman of compassion to the wretched and distressed? Likewise your mother, faithful to her husband, has gone to heaven, my child.
brahmapuran:110:152	In my view neither Lopamudra nor Arundhati equals her. By his bones all the gods are ever victorious and happy;
brahmapuran:110:153	he has gained abundant fame, and your mother has made it imperishable; by you, their son, it has been done everywhere — nothing higher has been done.
brahmapuran:110:154	You should protect those fallen from heaven in fear of your might; you should save the immortals who are bewildered by fear of you. There is no merit anywhere greater than saving the distressed.
brahmapuran:110:155	As long as one's fame shines beautifully in the human world, for so many days one who has gone to heaven dwells in the other world unchanged, each day counting as years.
brahmapuran:110:156	They alone are dead here who have no fame; they alone are blind who lack learning; those given to generosity are not eunuchs; those given to dharma are not to be pitied.
Hearing the words of the god of gods, the sage became calm; with joined palms, bowing to the Lord, he said:

To those who, devoted to my good, sometimes help me by words, thoughts and deeds — for their good and for others here, I bow to Soma, worshipped by the gods and others.
brahmapuran:110:159	May Shiva fulfil the wishes of those by whom I was protected and raised, of the same lineage and the same dharma; I ever bow to the one crowned with the young moon.
brahmapuran:110:160	Those by whom I was always raised like a mother and father, O Lord — let a holy place arise in the three worlds by their name, O god of gods.
brahmapuran:110:161	Then their fame will arise and I will be free of debt to them. Whatever regions of the gods and holy places there are on earth,
brahmapuran:110:162	let the deities agree that this is greater than them; then I, stainless, will forgive the gods' offence.
Then, in the presence of the gods, he spoke words heard by the gods before the thousand-eyed and the rest; the gods too accepted with respect the words spoken by the son of Dadhichi.
Knowing the child's intellect, humility, learning, valour, strength, daring, truthful speech, devotion to his parents and purity of feeling, Shankara then spoke to Pippalada:
Child, whatever dear desire you have, even what is dear to the gods, you will obtain; speak what is auspicious and set your mind on nothing else.

May those steadfast in dharma who bathe in the Ganga and behold your lotus feet, O great Lord, obtain all desires fully, and at the end of their bodies come to Shiva's state.
brahmapuran:110:167	My father has reached your state, and my mother, Lord; the pippalas and the immortals have found happiness seeing you, lord of lords; may they see you and go to your state.
Saying "So be it" to Pippalada, the god of gods Maheshvara, welcoming him, spoke together with the gods.
The gods too, joyful and freed from the fear he had caused, all said this to the son of Dadhichi in Shiva's presence:

What the gods wished has surely been done by you; the command of the god of gods, the ornament of the three worlds, has been kept.
brahmapuran:110:171	You asked before for others and not for yourself, O brahmin; therefore name something else and we will give it.
The hosts of gods said this again and again to the best of brahmins; Pippalada, with joined palms, first bowing to Shambhu and the gods, to Uma and the pippalas, said:

I wish to see my parents, who have always been only words to me. Blessed are those living beings in the world who remain under the care of mother and father,
brahmapuran:110:174	ever devoted to serving them, awaiting the command of their feet; having obtained senses, body, family, strength, intellect and form,
brahmapuran:110:175	one becomes fulfilled in their service. For beasts and birds too the sight of a mother is easy;
brahmapuran:110:176	it is hard for me — what is the fruit of this sin, I ask? If it were hard for all and everyone,
brahmapuran:110:177	it would not be easy; there is no other sinner than me. If I obtain merely the sight of them, O best of gods,
brahmapuran:110:178	the fruit of deeds of mind, speech and body will be obtained. Those who do not see their parents are not born into existence; who can count their great sins?
Hearing the sage's words, the gods consulted together: "Your parents, the auspicious couple, mounted on an excellent celestial car,
longing to see you — you will see them today, surely; give up dejection, greed and delusion and calm your mind."
Look, look, the best of gods said to the son of Dadhichi: mounted on an excellent celestial car, heavenly, adorned with gold,
longing to see you, your parents, the auspicious couple, fanned by the women of the gods and praised by Kinnaras.
Seeing his mother and father, he bowed in Shiva's presence; his eyes full of tears of joy, he somehow said to them:
Other sons, upholders of their families, save their parents; but I was merely the cause of splitting my mother's womb; even so, out of delusion, I, most wicked, wished to see them.
Looking at them, he could not speak for sorrow; the gods and the mother and father said to Pippalada:
Blessed are you, son, in the worlds, whose fame has gone to heaven; you have seen the three-eyed god face to face and comforted the gods; through you, our son, the good worlds never decline.
Then a shower of flowers fell from heaven on his head, and a cry of victory raised by the gods arose, O great sage.
Having blessed his son, Dadhichi with his wife bowed to Shambhu, the Ganga and the gods, and said to his son:
Take a wife, be devoted to Shiva and serve the Ganga; beget sons and duly perform sacrifices with fees; then, fulfilled, my child, go to heaven for a long time.
I will do so, Pippalada said to Dadhichi; Dadhichi, having comforted his son again and again with his wife,
and taking leave of the hosts of gods, went again to heaven. The gods all said hastily to Pippalada:
Pacify the Kritya, blessings on you, and the great fire born of her.
Pippalada said to them: "I cannot restrain her; I will not speak falsely; you speak to the Kritya.
Seeing me, that very fierce one will do the opposite." The gods went to her and spoke of pacification,
and to the fire as they liked; the two said "No: I was created by the brahmin to devour all,
and so was the fire born of me; how could it be otherwise? The five great elements, the unmoving and the moving —
know all to be in our mouth; nothing remains to be said." Having consulted with me, the gods spoke again to both:
Let both of you devour everything in due order. The mare then said this to the gods; hear, O Narada:
By your wish, O best of gods, everything is to be my food.
